title: SASA 2: Learners, admission and discipline
description: Admission rules, the learner code of conduct, suspension and expulsion, the corporal punishment ban, searches and drug testing, and the RCL under the South African Schools Act.

lessons.title: Admission: who may be turned away, and why not
lessons.summary: Non-discrimination, the ban on admission tests and fee conditions, the admission policy and appeals.
lessons.body:
## 🚪 The starting point: admit without unfair discrimination

SASA s5(1), as substituted by BELA s4, says a public school **must admit learners** and serve their educational requirements for the duration of their school attendance **without unfairly discriminating in any way**. This rests on the right to equality (Constitution s9) and the right to a basic education (Constitution s29).

This lesson is about public schools. Independent schools set their own admission rules, within the Constitution and their registration conditions.

## 🚫 Three things a school may never do

### 📝 No admission tests

The SGB may not administer any test related to admission, or direct or authorise the principal or anyone else to do so (SASA s5(2)). A school may not make a learner write a maths test, or attend a trial day that decides admission.

### 💰 No fee or contract conditions

SASA s5(3) says no learner may be refused admission because the parent:

1. Is unable to pay, or has not paid, school fees (s5(3)(a)).
2. Does not subscribe to the mission statement of the school (s5(3)(b)).
3. Has refused to sign a contract waiving any claim for damages arising out of the education of the learner (s5(3)(c)).

Example: a parent at the gate says "I cannot afford the fees this year." The school may not refuse the application on that basis. Fee exemptions are dealt with separately (see the School finances modules).

### 📄 Missing documents are not a reason to keep a child out

BELA s4 inserted s5(1A) and (1B): a learner whose parent has not provided required documents must still be allowed to attend school, and the principal must advise the parent to secure the documents.

## 🏫 The admission policy

The SGB determines the school's admission policy, subject to SASA, the Constitution and provincial law (SASA s5(5)). The BELA version of s5(5) adds that:

- The SGB must consider the needs of the broader community in the education district, the best interests of the child, other accessible schools, the school's resources and available space.
- The HOD, after consulting the SGB, has **final authority to admit** a learner.
- The SGB must review the policy every three years, or when circumstances change, or at the HOD's request.

> ⚠️ Watch out: The BELA changes to admission (BELA s4) and language (BELA s5) were the two clauses held back for consultation and linked to national norms and standards. Ask your district office which parts of the new s5 are in force for your province and which provincial admission regulations apply before you rely on them.

## 📮 Appeals

A learner or parent refused admission may appeal to the MEC (SASA s5(9)). Under the BELA wording the appeal must be lodged within 14 days of receiving the refusal, and the MEC must decide within 14 days (s5(9) and (10)). Applications are made to the education department as the HOD determines (s5(7)), and a refusal must be in writing with reasons (s5(8)).

> 💡 Tip: Always give the parent the refusal in writing, with the reason and how to appeal. It protects the school and the family.

## ✅ Key points

- A public school must admit learners without unfair discrimination (s5(1)).
- No admission tests (s5(2)) and no refusal for unpaid fees, the mission statement or a refused indemnity (s5(3)).
- A learner without documents may still attend while the parent gets them (s5(1A)).
- The SGB sets the admission policy, but the HOD has final authority to admit (s5(5) as amended).
- Refused learners may appeal to the MEC (s5(9)).

lessons.title: The code of conduct and the corporal punishment ban
lessons.summary: What the learner code of conduct must contain, exemptions, due process, and why no person may hit a learner.
lessons.body:
## 📜 Every public school needs a learner code of conduct

The SGB of a public school **must adopt a code of conduct for learners after consulting learners, parents and educators** (SASA s8(1) as substituted by BELA s7, and s20(1)(d)). It is subject to the Constitution, SASA and provincial law.

### 🎯 Its purpose

The code must aim to establish a **disciplined and purposeful school environment**, dedicated to improving and maintaining the quality of learning (s8(2)). BELA added that it must take into account the **diverse cultural beliefs, religious observances and medical circumstances** of learners.

The Minister may issue guidelines for SGBs adopting a code (s8(3)). National guidelines on codes of conduct and on school uniforms have been issued under this power, and provinces may add their own, so check the versions your district uses.

## 🙏 Exemptions

Every learner must obey the code (s8(4)(a)). But since BELA, the code **must contain an exemption provision** (s8(4)(b)). A learner or parent may apply to the SGB for exemption from certain provisions on grounds including cultural beliefs, religious observances and medical grounds.

1. The SGB must give its decision **within 14 days** of the application and give written reasons if it refuses (s8(4)(c)).
2. The learner or parent may appeal to the HOD **within 14 days** of the decision; the HOD must decide within 14 days and give written reasons (s8(4)(d)).

Example: a learner asks to wear a religious head covering that the uniform rules do not allow. The SGB must consider the application and answer in writing within 14 days.

## ⚖️ Due process is part of the code

The code must contain **due process provisions** protecting the learner and any other party in disciplinary proceedings (s8(5)). BELA added s8(5)(c): proceedings must be **age-appropriate**, in the **best interests of the learner**, and follow **natural justice, fairness and reasonableness**.

BELA s3 also inserted s4A(2): the SGB must make sure the code contains rules on **punctuality and regular attendance**.

> 💡 Tip: Review the code with your learners' representative council each year. Learners must be consulted (s8(1)), and they are more likely to respect rules they helped write.

## 🚫 Corporal punishment is abolished

SASA s10(1), as substituted by BELA s10, says corporal punishment is **abolished** and no person may inflict or impose corporal punishment on a learner **at a school, during a school activity, or in a hostel** accommodating learners of a school. "No person" includes educators, coaches, hostel staff, volunteers and parents acting at school.

A person who contravenes this is guilty of an **offence** and may be fined or imprisoned, or both, as a court decides (s10(2) as amended).

Related: SASA s10A, as amended by BELA s11, bans conducting or participating in initiation practices against a learner at school, during a school activity or in a hostel.

> ⚠️ Watch out: "A light smack" or making a learner do painful physical exercise as punishment can still be corporal punishment. Use the sanctions in the code of conduct instead and record what was done.

## ✅ Key points

- The SGB must adopt a learner code of conduct after consulting learners, parents and educators (s8(1)).
- The code must allow exemption applications on cultural, religious and medical grounds, with 14-day decisions and appeals (s8(4)).
- Disciplinary proceedings must be age-appropriate, fair and in the learner's best interests (s8(5)(c)).
- No person may impose corporal punishment at school, at a school activity or in a hostel; it is a criminal offence (s10).

lessons.title: Suspension and expulsion
lessons.summary: Precautionary suspension, the seven school day hearing rule, sanctions, who expels, and appeals.
lessons.body:
## ⚖️ Two different steps

SASA s9 separates **suspension** (keeping a learner out of school for a short time) from **expulsion** (removing the learner from the school). The SGB can suspend. Only the HOD can expel. This lesson covers public schools.

## ⏸️ Precautionary suspension before a hearing

The SGB may, on reasonable grounds and as a **precautionary measure**, suspend a learner who is **accused of serious misconduct** (SASA s9(1) as substituted by BELA s9). There are two routes:

1. **Representations first** (s9(1)(a)). For listed misconduct such as assault with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, harassment including online, repeated bullying, illegal possession of drugs or liquor, repeated disruption, serious exam transgressions, fraud, theft, possessing a dangerous object, possessing or distributing pornography, or sexual activity or sexual assault, the learner must first get a **reasonable opportunity to make representations** about the accusation.
2. **Immediate suspension** (s9(1)(b)). For serious crimes listed there, such as murder, rape or another sexual offence, robbery, or dealing in drugs, committed on school premises or at a school activity, where the learner has been **formally charged by the SAPS**, the SGB **must** suspend immediately without first hearing representations.

## 🗓️ The hearing and its timelines

- The SGB must hold the disciplinary hearing **within seven school days** after suspending the learner (s9(1A)).
- If it does not, it needs the **HOD's approval** to continue the suspension (s9(1B)).

At the hearing, follow the code of conduct, its due process rules and the provincial rules on serious misconduct and disciplinary proceedings that the MEC must publish (s9(3)). The proceedings must be age-appropriate and fair (s8(5)(c)). In practice this means written notice of the charges, time to prepare, the parent present, the right to be heard and to question witnesses, and a written outcome.

## 🔨 Sanctions after a guilty finding

If the learner is found guilty, the SGB may (s9(1C)):

- Suspend the learner as a sanction for **not longer than seven school days**, or impose another sanction in the code of conduct; or
- **Recommend expulsion** to the HOD.

The HOD must decide on a recommended expulsion **within 14 days** of receiving the recommendation (s9(1D)). While waiting, the SGB may suspend the learner, or extend the suspension, for **up to 14 days** (s9(1E)).

## 🏛️ Expulsion and appeals

A learner may be expelled **only by the HOD**, and only if found guilty of serious misconduct after proceedings under s8 (s9(2)).

- If the HOD decides not to expel, the HOD may impose a suitable sanction after consulting the SGB, or refer the matter back to the SGB for a sanction short of expulsion, which the SGB must implement (s9(8) to (10)).
- An expelled learner or parent may **appeal to the MEC within 14 days** of receiving notice of the expulsion (s9(4)).
- While an appeal is pending, the HOD must decide how the learner will keep getting education (s9(6) and (7)).
- If a learner of compulsory school age is expelled, the HOD must arrange placement at another public school (s9(5)).

> ⚠️ Watch out: The seven school day and 14 day clocks are short. Diarise them the moment a suspension starts. A late hearing without HOD approval can make the suspension unlawful.

> 💡 Tip: Provincial rules on serious misconduct may not yet reflect the BELA list in s9(1). Ask your district which provincial notice applies.

## ✅ Key points

- The SGB may suspend as a precaution; only the HOD may expel (s9(1) and (2)).
- Most accusations need representations first; SAPS-charged serious crimes require immediate suspension (s9(1)(a) and (b)).
- The hearing must be held within seven school days, or the HOD must approve continued suspension (s9(1A) and (1B)).
- A sanction suspension is capped at seven school days; the HOD decides expulsion within 14 days (s9(1C) and (1D)).
- Expulsion appeals go to the MEC within 14 days (s9(4)).

lessons.title: Searches, drug testing and the RCL
lessons.summary: When and how a learner may be searched or tested under section 8A, and the representative council of learners.
lessons.body:
## 🔍 Dangerous objects, liquor and drugs

SASA s8A(1), as amended by BELA s8, says no person may bring a **dangerous object or a drug** onto school premises, or have one at school or during a school activity, unless the principal has authorised it for legitimate educational purposes (for example, a science experiment).

## 🧳 Searching learners

The **principal or his or her delegate** may, at random, search a learner, a group of learners, or their property for liquor, dangerous objects or drugs, if a **fair and reasonable suspicion** has been established that such items may be found at school or that learners have them (s8A(2)).

Before searching, the principal must consider all relevant factors, including the best interests, safety and health of the learners, any reasonable evidence and all relevant information received. The search must be proportionate to the suspected activity (s8A(3)).

For a search of a learner's person (s8A(4)):

- It must be done by a person of the **same gender** as the learner.
- It must be done in a **private area**, not in view of other learners.
- **One adult witness of the same gender** must be present.
- It may **not** extend to a body cavity search.

Seized items must be labelled and handed to the police immediately, or taken to the nearest police station, and the police must give a receipt (s8A(5) to (7)).

## 🧪 Drug and alcohol testing

The principal or delegate may administer a **urine or other non-invasive test** to a learner or group reasonably suspected of using liquor or drugs (s8A(8)). The test must be by a person of the same gender, in private, with one adult same-gender witness, using a device identified by the Minister (s8A(9) and (11)).

The parent must, where practicable, be told **within one working day** that a search or test was done, and the learner and parent must be told the result as soon as it is available (s8A(10)).

A learner found with liquor, a dangerous object or any drug, or who tests positive, may face disciplinary proceedings under the code of conduct (s8A(12) and (13)). The school may not itself institute criminal proceedings against the learner on that basis (s8A(14)).

> ⚠️ Watch out: A search without a fair and reasonable suspicion, or a strip search in front of a class, breaks s8A and the learner's rights to privacy and dignity. Write down the reason for the search before you start.

## 🗣️ The representative council of learners (RCL)

Every public school enrolling learners in **grade 8 and higher** must establish a representative council of learners (SASA s11(1)). The MEC may publish guidelines on how RCLs are established and elected and what they do (s11(2)), and may exempt special schools where an RCL is not practical (s11(3)).

The RCL elects the learner members of the SGB (s23(4)), who serve for up to one year (s31(2)). Learner members who are minors may not sign contracts for the school or vote on resolutions that impose liabilities on the school (s32).

> 💡 Tip: Use the RCL as a real partner. Consult it on the code of conduct (s8(1)) and on safety, and invite it to the yearly meeting with learners required by s18(2)(b).

## ✅ Key points

- Searches need a fair and reasonable suspicion and must be private, same-gender and witnessed (s8A(2) to (4)).
- Drug tests must be non-invasive, private and use an approved device, and parents must be informed (s8A(8) to (11)).
- Seized items go to the police; the school disciplines under the code but may not lay criminal charges itself (s8A(5), (13), (14)).
- Schools with grade 8 and up must have an RCL, which elects the learner SGB members (s11(1), s23(4)).

questions.text: A parent cannot pay school fees. May the public school refuse to admit her child for that reason?

options.text: Yes, if the fees were approved at a parents meeting
No, a learner may not be refused admission because the parent cannot pay fees
Yes, but only in grade 8 and higher
Only if the SGB approves the refusal

questions.explanation: SASA s5(3)(a): no learner may be refused admission because the parent is unable to pay or has not paid school fees.

questions.text: Which admission practice does SASA forbid?

options.text: Requiring an admission test
Asking for a birth certificate
Having a written admission policy
Giving written reasons for a refusal

questions.explanation: SASA s5(2): the SGB may not administer any test related to admission, or direct anyone else to do so.

questions.text: Under the BELA wording, within what period must a parent appeal a refusal of admission to the MEC?

options.text: 30 days
7 school days
14 days
90 days

questions.explanation: SASA s5(9) as substituted by BELA s4: the appeal to the MEC must be made within 14 days of receiving the refusal.

questions.text: Within how many days must the SGB decide on an application for exemption from part of the code of conduct?

options.text: 7 days
30 days
Before the next SGB meeting
14 days

questions.explanation: SASA s8(4)(c) as inserted by BELA s7: the SGB must communicate its decision within 14 days and give written reasons for a refusal.

questions.text: A hostel supervisor smacks a learner for breaking curfew in the school hostel. What is the legal position?

options.text: It is corporal punishment and an offence
It is allowed because the hostel is not a classroom
It is allowed with parental consent
It is a matter only for the code of conduct

questions.explanation: SASA s10(1) and (2) as substituted by BELA s10: no person may inflict corporal punishment on a learner at a school, during a school activity or in a hostel, and doing so is an offence.

questions.text: After suspending a learner as a precaution, within what period must the SGB hold the disciplinary hearing?

options.text: 14 days
Seven school days
One month
Before the end of the term

questions.explanation: SASA s9(1A): disciplinary proceedings must be held within seven school days after the suspension, otherwise HOD approval is needed to continue it (s9(1B)).

questions.text: Who may expel a learner from a public school?

options.text: The SGB chairperson
The principal
The SGB disciplinary committee
The Head of Department

questions.explanation: SASA s9(2): a learner may be expelled only by the HOD and only if found guilty of serious misconduct after proceedings under s8.

questions.text: A learner on school premises is formally charged by the SAPS with robbery. What must the SGB do?

options.text: Wait for the criminal trial before acting
Suspend the learner immediately without first hearing representations
Expel the learner immediately
Hold a hearing within 14 days before any suspension

questions.explanation: SASA s9(1)(b) as substituted by BELA s9: for listed serious crimes on school premises where the learner is formally charged by the SAPS, the SGB must suspend immediately without first hearing representations.

questions.text: Which requirement applies when the principal searches a learner's person under section 8A?

options.text: It may be done in the classroom if quick
Any staff member may search any learner
It must be by a person of the same gender, in private, with one adult same-gender witness
It must be done by the police only

questions.explanation: SASA s8A(4): a search of a learner's person must be by a person of the same gender, in a private area, with one adult witness of the same gender, and may not include a body cavity search.

questions.text: Which public schools must have a representative council of learners?

options.text: Every public school enrolling learners in grade 8 and higher
Only schools with more than 500 learners
Only schools that apply for section 21 functions
Every public school, including primary schools ending at grade 7

questions.explanation: SASA s11(1): an RCL must be established at every public school enrolling learners in the eighth grade and higher.
